name: PVB (Polyvinyl Butyral)
chemical_makeup: Polyvinyl butyral — a polyvinyl acetal made by reacting polyvinyl alcohol with butyraldehyde, industrially the interlayer of laminated safety glass. Filament grades (Polymaker PolySmooth, Prusament PVB) are blended rather than pure PVB to make them extrudable, which is why prints are translucent rather than glass-clear. The defining trait is solubility in isopropyl alcohol, enabling vapour or brush smoothing.
summary: A PLA-easy filament whose whole reason for existing is post-processing: brief exposure to isopropyl alcohol melts the layer lines into a glossy, near-glass finish, and the same solvent welds parts together seamlessly. In exchange it is brittle in Z, hygroscopic, heat-limited, and dissolves on contact with alcohol or many household cleaners.

printing.notes: Essentially a PLA profile. Polymaker quotes 190-220 °C and up to 200 mm/s at a 15 mm³/s volumetric ceiling; Prusa quotes 215 ± 10 °C and requires a heated bed at 65-85 °C. Open-frame machines are fine and an enclosure brings no benefit. Run full part cooling — surface quality before smoothing directly determines how good the smoothed finish is. Unfilled, so a brass nozzle is fine.

feeding.notes: Rigid and PLA-like in the feed path, so no drive-system or material-station restriction applies; PVB is not named in Bambu's material table but is absent from the AMS notes' excluded list and is neither flexible nor abrasive. The practical caution for a multi-day AMS job is hygroscopy rather than feeding: PVB should be resealed between prints and not left sitting in an unsealed unit. Enclosure: Bambu's heat-creep guidance names PLA as the material to run with the upper cover removed, and PVB runs a PLA-class profile (190-225 °C, full part cooling) at Tg 70 °C, so enclosure_open_for_cooling is recorded true by direct analogy — no PVB-specific door-open statement was found, and Polymaker simply states no enclosure is needed for PolySmooth.

drying.dryness_validation: No popping or crackling at the nozzle; no visible steam; a consistent glossy extrudate with no foaming or surface bubbles
drying.notes: Polymaker describes PVB as more hygroscopic than PLA, and Prusa recommends 60 °C for 4 h whenever the spool has not been stored sealed. Wet PVB prints rough, which is doubly costly here because smoothing amplifies surface defects it cannot fill.

storage.recommendations: Always reseal in a bag or drybox with silica gel between prints; do not leave a spool on the printer for days. Keep well away from alcohols, perfumes and solvent-based cleaners, which attack the filament as readily as they attack the prints.

price.notes: Roughly double standard PLA. Prusament PVB is $24.99 per 500 g spool (~$50/kg); the wider market sits around $33-45/kg.

recommended: artistic pieces intended for IPA vapour smoothing to a glass-like finish
multi-part assemblies bonded seamlessly by alcohol welding
not_recommended: structural or load-bearing parts (weak layer adhesion, brittle fracture)
anything contacting alcohol, perfume or household cleaners (the material dissolves)
outdoor parts (no UV stabilisation, low heat resistance)
parts that must hold tolerances after any solvent contact

properties.notes: Density 1.10 g/cm³ at 23 °C and Tg 70 °C (Polymaker TDS). HDT 68.0 °C @0.45 MPa and 66.3 °C @1.8 MPa (Polymaker); Prusa and FacFox cite roughly 60 °C. The tensile range spans the anisotropy rather than a brand spread: Polymaker measured 44.1 ± 0.8 MPa in XY but only 18.4 ± 1.2 MPa in Z — the recommended value is the XY figure, and the minimum is the interlayer figure that governs real part strength. Max service temperature (~50-55 °C) is inferred from Tg, not measured. Shrinkage is not stated in any datasheet found; it is low in practice.

compatibility.notes: PVB welds to itself chemically rather than thermally: a wipe of isopropyl alcohol on both faces fuses printed parts into an effectively seamless assembly, which is the standard way to build objects larger than the build plate in this material. No vendor guidance was found recommending co-printing PVB with PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, PA, PC, PP, TPU, TPE, HIPS, PVA, BVOH, PCTG or PET, and no structural bond to any of them is documented (unverified for every pairing). For soluble supports Polymaker documents PolyDissolve S1, a PVA-type material, as the pairing for PolySmooth. PVB is not used as a support for other filaments.

plate_recommendations.notes: Polymaker lists textured and smooth PEI (and PC) as suitable. Bed 60-70 °C is the practical sweet spot, though up to 85 °C is tolerated. Glue is optional rather than required and no PVB-specific release agent guidance was found — if the part bonds too hard, fall back to the PETG-family remedies (thin glue-stick layer as a separator) and let the plate cool fully before removal.

primary_emissions: isopropyl alcohol vapour (during smoothing, not printing)
emissions.notes: No dedicated UFP/VOC study of PVB printing was found; extrusion emissions are expected to be low and PLA-like given the 190-220 °C nozzle window (unverified). The real hazard here is post-processing rather than printing: Polymaker explicitly requires a well-ventilated area during isopropyl alcohol smoothing to avoid inhaling IPA vapour, which is also flammable. Ventilation is recorded as 'recommended' for the print itself and should be read as effectively required for the smoothing step, away from any ignition source.

safety_notes: Isopropyl alcohol smoothing is the dominant safety consideration: IPA vapour is flammable and an inhalation irritant. Smooth in a ventilated space or fume box, keep the container closed between uses, and keep it clear of the printer's hot end and any spark source. Finished parts remain alcohol-sensitive, so they cannot be disinfected or cleaned with alcohol wipes.
additional_notes: Layer adhesion is the material's defining weakness and the main reason it is a display material rather than a functional one — Z tensile is only 42 % of XY. Alcohol welding partly compensates by letting a part be split and reassembled so that loads run in-plane.

provenance.conflicts: HDT: Polymaker's TDS gives 68.0 °C @0.45 MPa (66.3 °C @1.8 MPa) while Prusa and FacFox cite ~60 °C — the datasheet value is recorded and the 60-68 °C spread noted. Tg: Polymaker states 70 °C; FacFox only describes it qualitatively as 'comparable to PLA', which would imply nearer 60 °C — the datasheet figure is treated as primary. Bed temperature: Polymaker allows 25-85 °C (heated bed optional) while Prusa requires a heated bed at 65-85 °C; the union is recorded with 70 °C recommended. Speed: Polymaker's 200 mm/s ceiling conflicts with community guidance of 40-60 mm/s for good surface finish. Strength: FacFox claims PVB tensile strength exceeds ABS and PETG, which is only defensible for XY values and directly contradicts the 18.4 MPa Z figure. Max service temperature is inferred, not measured, and no UV or weathering data exists for PVB at all — those scores are reasoned from the absence of any UV stabilisation plus the low heat ceiling.
